name: Etta James
description: Etta James (born Jamesetta Hawkins on January 25, 1938, in Los Angeles, California; died January 20, 2012, in Riverside, California) was an American singer who bridged rhythm and blues, soul, and rock and roll. Discovered as a teenager by bandleader Johnny Otis, she first hit with “The Wallflower” in 1955. In 1960 she signed with Chicago's Chess Records; her debut album, At Last!, appeared that year on the Chess imprint Argo, and its title ballad became her signature song. Across roughly eighteen years at Chess she recorded “I'd Rather Go Blind,” “Tell Mama,” and “Something's Got a Hold on Me,” sustaining her career through years of addiction and repeated comebacks. In 1993 she was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

name: Ernie Banks
aliases: Mr. Cub; Ernest Banks; Mr. Sunshine
description: Ernie Banks (January 31, 1931, Dallas, Texas – January 23, 2015, Chicago) — 'Mr. Cub' — was the first Black player in Chicago Cubs history and the joyful face of baseball on Chicago's North Side for two generations. He came up through the Kansas City Monarchs of the Negro Leagues, served in the U.S. Army (1951–1953), and debuted for the Cubs on September 17, 1953, playing his entire nineteen-season major-league career in Chicago, first as a power-hitting shortstop and later at first base. He won back-to-back National League MVP awards in 1958 and 1959 and finished with 512 home runs, 2,583 hits, and 1,636 runs batted in. His signature greeting, 'Let's play two,' became part of the city's vocabulary. He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame on the first ballot in 1977; the Cubs retired his No. 14 in 1982, raised his statue outside Wrigley Field in 2008, and in 2013 he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

name: Empire
description: Empire, created by Lee Daniels and Danny Strong and produced by Imagine Television with 20th Century Fox Television, aired on Fox from January 7, 2015, to April 21, 2020 — six seasons built around Lucious Lyon's hip-hop empire and the family fighting to inherit it, with Taraji P. Henson's Cookie Lyon becoming, in first-season critical coverage, the show's defining performance. Its ratings were a genuine phenomenon: the premiere drew nearly ten million viewers, the first-season finale about seventeen million, and contemporary reporting described it as breaking a twenty-three-year record — the only scripted series to grow its total audience in each of its first five episodes. Original music functioned as a narrative engine rather than decoration, a network-scale bet on hip-hop as prime-time's center. Its Chicago connection is production, and this graph counts production: set in New York, Empire was filmed in Chicago, its pilot shot at Cinespace Chicago Film Studios in March 2014, and trade coverage grouped it with the city's other standing series in making Chicago a top television production hub under the Illinois incentive.

name: Englewood
description: Englewood is an official Chicago community area on the South Side, crossed by the 63rd Street corridor that CTL's place research treats as a central spine of Black Chicago's twentieth century. Its documented anchors include Kennedy-King College at 6301 S. Halsted and the Halsted and 63rd Red Line stations; the 63rd Red Line station at 220 W. 63rd Street formally opened on September 26, 1969, on the Dan Ryan branch. The Metropolitan Planning Council's 2023 report depicts the Dan Ryan Expressway as a 14-lane barrier that bisected South Side communities, with Englewood among the areas physically severed. The neighborhood's commercial past is documented at property level: the seven-story Sears store at 6233 S. Halsted opened in 1934 and closed in January 1976, with contemporary reporting already disputing whether its departure meant the mall's collapse. Englewood's institutions — churches named as trusted partners in LISC Chicago's 2019 Micro-Market Recovery Program among them — make it a load-bearing geography for CTL's corridor research. name: Eve Ewing

description: Eve L. Ewing (born 1986) is a Chicago sociologist, poet, and author whose work studies — and sings — her hometown. Raised in the Logan Square neighborhood and educated in Chicago Public Schools, she took her undergraduate degree in English at the University of Chicago (AB'08), taught middle-school English in CPS, and earned an Ed.M. (2013) and Ed.D. (2016) at the Harvard Graduate School of Education. Her poetry collection Electric Arches (2017) moves between memoir, speculation, and visual art; Ghosts in the Schoolyard (2018) examines the 2013 Chicago school closings — the largest mass school closure in American history — and what the closed buildings meant to the South Side communities that loved them. 1919 (2019) answers the Chicago race riot with poems. She wrote Marvel's Ironheart series, giving Riri Williams, a teenage genius from the South Shore, her solo title. At the University of Chicago she was an assistant professor in the Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy, and Practice (2018–2022) and is, from 2023, an associate professor in the Department of Race, Diaspora, and Indigeneity. Original Sins, her study of racism's construction in American schooling, appeared in 2025.

name: Ewart Abner
description: Ewart Abner (Ewart G. Abner Jr., 1923–1997) was the executive who ran two of the most important Black-owned record companies in American history. Trained as an accountant, he worked at Chance Records before joining Chicago's Vee-Jay Records — founded in Gary, Indiana, in 1953 by Vivian Carter and James C. Bracken — where he rose from manager to vice president to president of what became the largest Black-owned label of its era. Vee-Jay's subsidiary labels (Falcon, Conrad, Tollie, and Abner) took their names in part from their principals' middle names. The label's collapse in the mid-1960s followed the Beatles licensing episode, Capitol Records lawsuits, and, in NPR-reported accounts, Abner's gambling losses and payroll schemes. Abner later became president of Motown Records in 1973 and managed the Supremes, the Temptations, the Jackson 5, and Stevie Wonder; AllMusic calls him a president of two pioneering Black-owned labels, Vee-Jay and Motown.

name: Eugene Sawyer
description: Eugene Sawyer Jr. (September 3, 1934 – January 19, 2008) was Chicago's 53rd mayor and its second Black mayor. Born in Greensboro, Alabama, he graduated from Alabama State University in 1956 with a chemistry degree, taught briefly in Mississippi, and moved to Chicago in 1957, working for the city water department from 1959 while rising through the Sixth Ward Democratic organization. Elected 6th Ward alderman in February 1971, he was, by 1987, the City Council's longest-serving Black alderman. After Harold Washington died in office on November 25, 1987, the council chose Sawyer as acting mayor in a tumultuous late-night session; he was sworn in at 4:01 a.m. on December 2, 1987. His tenure enacted Washington's 1988 budget and carried Washington-backed measures into law, including the 1988 Human Rights Ordinance. He lost the February 1989 Democratic primary to Richard M. Daley and left office that April.

name: Everybody Hates Chris
description: Everybody Hates Chris, created by Chris Rock and Ali LeRoi and narrated by Rock from his own teenage years in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, premiered on UPN on September 22, 2005, moved to The CW in the UPN/WB merger, and ended on May 8, 2009 — four seasons set in 1982–87, with Tyler James Williams as the young Chris, bussed to a whiter school across town and holding a family's economics in his head at all times. Its premiere was reported as the highest-rated comedy premiere in UPN's history. The form was the argument: a period, single-camera, narrated sitcom at a moment when the Black family comedy was presumed to be multi-camera and present-tense. It was nominated for the Golden Globe for Best Television Series — Musical or Comedy and for three Emmy Awards, and won NAACP Image Awards for LeRoi's writing and for Tichina Arnold and Tyler James Williams. In this graph it stands as the shelf's proof that the Black sitcom could do memory — could be set deliberately in the past and narrated like a memoir — a decade before the form's streaming-era flowering.

name: Essence Communications
description: Publisher of Essence magazine, essence.com, and the Essence Festival of Culture; founded 1968 by Edward Lewis, Clarence O. Smith, Cecil Hollingsworth, and Jonathan Blount; majority Black-owned under Lewis/Smith for 35 years; Time Inc. took 49% (2000) then full control (2005); sold to Essence Ventures in January 2018, returning to Black ownership; weathered COVID-era furloughs (2020); independent reviews of 2020 workplace allegations found no misconduct.

name: Essence Ventures
aliases: Essence Ventures / Sundial Media & Technology Group; Essence Ventures LLC
description: Black-owned holding company founded 2017 by Shea Moisture co-founder Richelieu Dennis; acquired Essence Communications from Time Inc. (January 2018); portfolio includes ESSENCE, Girls United, ESSENCE Studios, the Essence Festival of Culture, Afropunk, Beautycon, NaturallyCurly, and (from April 2024) Refinery29; operates as a division of Sundial Media Group.

name: Eyes on the Prize rights blackout
description: The rights-driven withdrawal of Henry Hampton/Blackside's civil-rights documentary series Eyes on the Prize: by the mid-1990s rebroadcasts and home-video distribution were halted as archival footage, photo, and music licenses expired; a 2005 Ford Foundation grant ($600,000) plus Richard Gilder's gift ($250,000) funded the renewal effort; the series returned to PBS in October 2006 and to educational DVD that fall, with no archival material removed or altered.

name: Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument established
aliases: Till National Monument; Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument
description: July 25, 2023 presidential proclamation (Joseph R. Biden Jr., 54 U.S.C. 320301) establishing the NPS-managed national monument across three sites: Graball Landing (Glendora, MS), the Tallahatchie County Second District Courthouse (Sumner, MS), and Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ (Chicago). Signed on what would have been Emmett Till's 82nd birthday; approximately 5.70 acres.

name: Elizabeth Lindsay Davis
description: Clubwoman, historian, and settlement founder (1855-1944). Born in Peoria, Illinois, oldest of six; graduated Princeton Township High School with high honors in 1873; teacher; married podiatrist Dr. William H. Davis (1885); moved to Chicago (1893). First secretary of the Ida B. Wells Club; co-founded the Phyllis Wheatley Woman's Club (March 1896, president 28 years); NACW national organizer for twelve years; official historian of the Illinois Federation of Colored Women's Clubs; founded the Phyllis Wheatley Home for Girls settlement house (1908). Authored 'The Story of the Illinois Federation of Colored Women's Clubs, 1900-1922' (1922) and 'Lifting as We Climb' (1933, history of the NACW).

name: Englewood branch (now Ashland branch, CTA Green Line)
description: CTA Green Line branch opened in stages 1905–1907 (State, Wentworth, Princeton, Harvard, Parnell, Racine, Loomis); Loomis replaced by the Ashland/63rd terminal (opened May 6, 1969); branch closed for the 1994–1996 Green Line renovation and reopened May 12, 1996 renamed the Ashland branch. Remaining stations: Ashland/63rd and Halsted.

name: Englewood commercial district (63rd & Halsted)
description: Historic shopping district at 63rd & Halsted, Englewood. Once Chicago's second-busiest shopping district outside downtown; anchored by Sears, Wieboldt's, and the 3,200-seat Southtown Theatre. Converted to a pedestrian mall in 1964; declined after anchors left.

name: El Grotto Supper Club
description: Supper club at 6412 S. Cottage Grove, in Chicago's Pershing Hotel (Woodlawn), operating 1944-1947. Hosted Ivie Anderson, saxophonist George Auld, and singer Ida James; billed as 'Harry Fields' El Grotto Supper Club'; served dinner to the Billikens; fielded a prize-winning float (1946). The Pershing Hotel's Beige Room opened in its space in December 1947. Documented in the University of Chicago Library's 'Researching Chicago Jazz Venues' guide from Chicago Defender citations.

name: Elman's Shoes
description: Shoe store on 63rd Street in Woodlawn, Chicago, documented in a 1955 photograph at 63rd and Maryland Avenue. The ‘Elman Shoe’ terrazzo name survives on the building's corner entrance; in the 1970s the space became Kham & Nate Shoes, shown in the 1976 film ‘Monkey Hustle.’

name: E.G. Woode small-business hub
description: Small-business hub at 1122 West 63rd Street, Englewood, Chicago (IL 60621), opened August 25, 2022, by E.G. Woode - a collective of architects, designers, entrepreneurs, and journeymen. The fully renovated building houses entrepreneurs of color including Powell's Barbershop, Marie|Wesley, Beehyyve, and Momentum Coffee. The operating company is structured as E.G. Woode L3C; in 2026 the city selected its proposal for a mixed-use complex across two West Englewood sites.

name: Englewood Academy High School
description: Former Chicago Public Schools neighborhood high school at 6201 S. Stewart Ave., Englewood. Phased out beginning 2005; last class graduated 2008; building reopened for TEAM Englewood Community Academy and Urban Prep Academy. TEAM Englewood was later consolidated with Harper, Hope, and Robeson into Englewood STEM High School (opened September 3, 2019).

name: Englewood Mall (pedestrian mall)
description: Pedestrianized shopping mall on Halsted at 63rd in Englewood (also called the Englewood Shopping Center): Halsted reportedly closed to automobiles in 1969, mall build-out circa 1973; host of community events under the Business Men's Association; replaced by the Kennedy-King College campus (opened 2007). Opening/conversion dates carry an explained conflict.

name: Englewood Square
description: Shopping center opened 2016 at the northwest corner of Halsted & 63rd on the former Englewood Mall footprint; developed by Leon Walker's DL3 Realty LP. Original tenants included Whole Foods (opened Sept 28, 2016; closed Nov 14, 2022), Starbucks, Chipotle, Villa, and Oak Street Health, with PNC Bank following.

name: Englewood Business Men's Association
description: Commercial association of Englewood, Chicago merchants — nearly 500 business men by the early 20th century — that paved and lit the 63rd & Halsted district and later spearheaded the Englewood Shopping Center's community integration under director Richard Drew (d. 1978).

name: Englewood Theatre
description: Englewood, Chicago movie house: ended burlesque and went movies-only on February 12, 1922 (starting with ‘Hail the Woman’); staged a public wedding on June 28, 1928; modernized in 1949; still advertising films in 1959. Demolition date unresolved in the sources.

name: Englewood Union Station site
description: Former major rail junction and passenger depot in Englewood, Chicago, served by the Rock Island, New York Central, Pennsylvania, and Nickel Plate railroads; closed to regular passenger service April 9, 1969 (1978 per Wikipedia — explained conflict); structure standing July 1979; site later a Norfolk Southern intermodal terminal. Distinct from the ‘Little Englewood’ C&WI station at 63rd & State.

name: E. David Ellington
description: Entertainment lawyer and new-media executive who co-founded NetNoir Inc. with Malcolm CasSelle in June 1995 - one of the first Afrocentric media websites, launched on AOL and the Web and the first outside company in AOL's Greenhouse Program. Born July 10, 1960, in New York; Adelphi (BA), Howard (master's), Georgetown (law); served on the House Subcommittee on Africa; founded the Law Offices of E. David Ellington in Los Angeles in the early 1990s; NetNoir president and CEO.

name: Earl 'Spanky' Smith Jr.
description: Acid house pioneer Earl Smith Jr. (c.1965-September 21, 2016), known as DJ Spank-Spank or Spanky. Founded Phuture with DJ Pierre and Herb Jackson in 1985; bought an old Roland TB-303 and created the 'burbling, squelchy' bass line behind 'Acid Tracks' (cassette circulation, then Trax Records, March 1987 - sometimes claimed as the first acid house record). Stayed with Phuture until the c.1990 split; issued solo tracks; Phuture reformed 1996. Died after a stroke earlier in 2016, leaving an unfinished album.

name: Elijah McCoy
description: Canadian-American inventor (May 2, 1844-October 10, 1929) whose automatic steam-engine lubricator gave rise to the phrase 'the real McCoy.' Son of George and Mildred McCoy, who escaped Kentucky slavery via the Underground Railroad to Colchester, Ontario; apprenticed in mechanical engineering at the University of Edinburgh as a teenager. Denied engineering work by racism, he worked as a locomotive fireman and oiler on the Michigan Central Railroad, then invented the automatic lubricator (patented 1872); by 1900 it was on almost all North American railroads. Held 57+ patents, including a 1916 graphite lubricator; founded the Elijah McCoy Manufacturing Company in 1920.

name: Emmit McHenry
description: Record describing Emmit McHenry (b. 1943), the entrepreneur and engineer who co-founded Network Solutions (1979) with Gary Desler, Ty Grigsby, and Ed Peters — the first domain-name registrar; later founded NetCom Solutions International and chairs Cycurion (Nasdaq: CYCU). (Canonical type is Institution — a TECH-001 merge artifact; type kept in place, flagged for coordinator review.)

name: Erin Reddick
description: Founder and CEO of ChatBlackGPT, a culturally informed AI platform providing perspectives from Black and African American communities, launched on Juneteenth 2024. Former tech roles at Amazon, Microsoft, and AWS; certified ChatGPT expert and prompt engineer; delivered the January 2025 MLK Winter Convocation keynote at Susquehanna University.

name: Eunice Walker Johnson
description: Businesswoman and fashion icon (1916–2010); secretary-treasurer of Johnson Publishing Company from its 1942 founding; named Ebony magazine; created the Ebony Fashion Fair (1958–2009), a traveling haute-couture fundraiser that toured ~180 cities and raised $50M+ for charity; founded Fashion Fair Cosmetics (1973), the first national makeup line for Black women.

name: Ethiopian Art Theatre
aliases: Ethiopian Art Players; Chicago Folk Theatre; Colored Folk Theatre
description: Short-lived (1922/1923–1925) Chicago-based Black theatre company of the Harlem Renaissance, founded by white director Raymond O'Neil and sponsored by Mrs. Sherwood Anderson; its all-Black performers staged European repertoire (Wilde's Salome, a jazz-accompanied Comedy of Errors) and Black-authored work, including Willis Richardson's The Chip Woman's Fortune — the first Black drama produced on Broadway (Frazee Theatre, May 7, 1923).

name: Easter best and church-hat fashion
description: Easter Sunday as the peak of Black church fashion - 'the Olympics of church fashion': new coordinated outfits for the whole family, elaborate hats ('crowns') for church mothers, children's Easter speeches and programs, and Easter dinner after service. Roots in the Reconstruction/post-Emancipation era, when Sunday best became a public statement of self-respect; biblical precedent in 1 Corinthians 11:15. Documented in Michael Cunningham's 2000 photo book 'Crowns: Portraits of Black Women in Church Hats' (adapted into a Regina Taylor stage play) and the Smithsonian Anacostia's 'Jubilee' exhibit.

name: Ebony Fashion Fair (Johnson Publishing Company)
aliases: Ebony Travelling Fashion Fair; Ebony Fashion Fair
description: Annual traveling fashion show created in Chicago in 1958 by Eunice Walker Johnson; the world's largest traveling fashion show, it exposed Black audiences — especially in segregated cities — to haute couture while platforming Black models and designers and raising $55 million for Black charities; final show 2009. Johnson also founded Fashion Fair Cosmetics (1973; the prior graph note said 1972).

name: Earl B. Dickerson
description: Chicago lawyer (1891-1986): first African American to earn a JD from the University of Chicago Law School (1920); general counsel (1921) and president (1952) of Supreme Life Insurance Company; first Black Democratic alderman on the Chicago City Council (2nd Ward, 1939-1943); orchestrated and argued Hansberry v. Lee (1940) before the U.S. Supreme Court; served on FDR’s first Fair Employment Practices Committee; president of the National Lawyers Guild (1951-1954); national NAACP board member; president of the Chicago Urban League; helped establish Burr Oak Cemetery (1927).

name: Elder Lucy Smith
description: Elder Lucy Smith (1874–1952), born Lucinda Madden in Woodstock, Georgia, was an African-American Pentecostal pastor and faith healer who founded All Nations Pentecostal Church in Chicago — the first church in the city founded by a woman pastor; her healing ministry drew 3,000 members and her funeral drew 60,000.

name: ECM Records
description: Record label of the Art Ensemble of Chicago’s classic albums (“Nice Guys,” “Full Force,” “Urban Bushmen,” “The Third Decade”).

name: Ethiopian Airlines launches Chicago O'Hare - Addis Ababa service (June 2018)
description: Inaugural nonstop service between Chicago O'Hare International Airport and Addis Ababa Bole International Airport; the first-ever direct scheduled passenger service between Chicago and Africa.

name: ECAC 33rd Anniversary Benefit Dinner (May 13, 2017)
description: Ethiopian Community Association of Chicago's 33rd anniversary benefit dinner at ECAC's Community Center, 1730 W Greenleaf Ave.

name: Emmett McBain
description: Chicago art director and designer; co-founder with Tom Burrell of Burrell McBain Advertising (1971); bought out by Burrell in 1974.

name: Englewood High School
description: Former Chicago public high school in Englewood; Larry Snelling’s alma mater.

name: Elgin, Illinois
description: Birthplace of Brandon Johnson (March 27, 1976).

name: East St. Louis, Illinois
description: City in St. Clair County, Illinois, across the Mississippi from St. Louis; Katherine Dunham's base from 1967.

name: Edward 'Big Ed' Jones
description: Lead figure of the Jones brothers' policy (numbers) enterprise in 1930s-40s Bronzeville; subject of the documentary 'King of Kings: Chasing Edward Jones.'

name: Eugene Williams
description: Black teenager, born in Georgia, a grocery porter living at 3921 Prairie Avenue; his drowning at the 29th Street Beach on July 27, 1919 ignited the Chicago Race Riot.

name: Ethel Darden
description: Black educator (1900–2011) born in Dallas, Texas; taught in Dallas schools for nearly two decades, moved to Chicago in 1942, and taught at Howalton Day School after her twin sister Doris Allen — a founder — enlisted her. Howalton grew out of Oneida Cockrell's pioneering preschool and kindergarten.

name: Edward H. Wright
description: Chicago attorney and politician; admitted to the Illinois bar in 1896 and elected a Cook County commissioner the same year; first president of the Cook County Bar Association (1914–1918).

name: Edward Lewis
description: Co-founder of Essence Communications Inc. (1968) with Clarence O. Smith, Cecil Hollingsworth, and Jonathan Blount; majority owner with Smith through a 35-year partnership; co-visionary of the Essence Music Festival.

name: Essence Festival of Culture
description: Annual festival launched 1995 in New Orleans for Essence's 25th anniversary; the nation's largest Black culture and music attraction, drawing roughly 500,000 attendees each year.

name: Ernest A. Griffin
description: Bronzeville funeral director who built Griffin Funeral Home, Ltd. with his wife Alyce; graduated Worsham College of Mortuary Science (1934) and conducted the final rites of Elijah Muhammad and Jesse Owens. Congressional Record (1995) spells his name 'Earnest' - see CTL-CFL-002125.

name: Elroy J. Duncan
description: Credited by some accounts with inventing and manufacturing the first hot comb (heated metal straightening comb) in America during the late 19th century.

name: Ebony magazine suspends print publication (2019-05)
description: Clear View Group suspends Ebony's print edition on May 24, 2019 (Spring 2019 last printed); the magazine relaunches in digital format in March 2021.

name: Elijah Thurston
description: Founder of New Covenant Missionary Baptist Church; grandfather of Rev. Stephen J. Thurston.

name: Elnathan Hall
description: Former administration building of Knoxville College: 126 years old, listed on the National Register of Historic Places; destroyed by fire November 4, 2024 (suspected set fire); remains razed by the city.

name: East Tennessee History Center
description: The East Tennessee History Center is a history center in Knoxville, Tennessee, at 601 South Gay Street. It houses three collections under one roof: the Museum of East Tennessee History, the Knox County Archive, and the Calvin M. McClung Historical Collection. Among its holdings, the center holds the official Knoxville College collection, making it the archival home of record for that Knoxville institution. The graph record dates the center's era from 2004 to the present, and its sources include the center's own research page and CultureTechLens batch research.

name: Eunice Trotter
description: Director of Indiana Landmarks' Black Heritage Preservation Program; called the King and King Funeral Home records a 'treasure trove' for historians and genealogists.

name: Edison Electric Light Company
description: Thomas Edison's electric-lighting company; hired Lewis Latimer in 1884 as a draftsman and expert witness in patent litigation; combined with Thomson-Houston in 1892 to form General Electric.

name: Epic Records
description: Major label; the success of 'French Kiss' brought Lil Louis a contract with Epic, for which he released two albums before leaving at his own instigation.

name: Emogene Taylor
description: Artist whom Julius F. Taylor met and married in Fargo, North Dakota; the couple later moved to Chicago and then to Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1895, where Taylor launched The Broad Ax.

name: Eugene D. Jackson
description: African-American electrical engineer and business consultant; co-founder of the National Black Network (1973) and founder of the National Association of Black Owned Broadcasters (1976).

name: Emma Reynolds
description: Nurse and physician; denied nursing-school admission in Chicago because she was Black — the catalyst for Provident Hospital's founding; member of Provident's first nursing graduating class (October 27, 1892); first Black woman to earn an MD from Northwestern's Woman's Medical School (1895).

name: Electric Light Orchestra
description: British rock band whose cover of 'Roll Over Beethoven' is counted among the song's most notable versions.

name: Evanston, Illinois
description: North Shore city; home base of the Haitian band Sakad and DJ Sagittarius.

name: Earl Ormes
description: Hotel manager; married cartoonist Jackie Ormes in 1936; they remained married 45 years until his death in 1976.

description: DJ and producer; with Rakim formed Eric B. & Rakim, whose 1986 single 'Eric B. Is President' was produced by Marley Marl and whose debut album Paid in Full was recorded in Marl's studio.

name: Ella Fitzgerald
description: Ella Fitzgerald was a jazz performer who received the NEA Jazz Masters Fellowship in 1985. She performed at Chicago's Regal Theater in Bronzeville, the premier South Side showcase for Black entertainment, appearing on the theater's documented roster of notable performers of the 1920s–40s. Fitzgerald's presence in the city extended beyond the stage: jazz photographer Samuel “Lonnie” Simmons photographed her among the performers and patrons of 1940s–50s Bronzeville nightlife, part of an 800-photograph cache later published in the book Bronzeville Nights: On the Town in Chicago's Black Metropolis (CityFiles Press, 2021).

name: Ezra Collective
description: Ezra Collective is a London jazz quintet — drummer and bandleader Femi Koleoso, his brother TJ Koleoso on bass, keyboardist Joe Armon-Jones, saxophonist James Mollison and trumpeter Ife Ogunjobi — whose members met through the Tomorrow's Warriors youth jazz programme. Fusing jazz with Afrobeat, hip-hop, calypso and soul, the group released its debut album, You Can't Steal My Joy, in 2019, featuring Jorja Smith and Loyle Carner. Its second album, Where I'm Meant To Be (2022), won the 2023 Mercury Prize — making Ezra Collective the first jazz act ever to win it — and in 2025 the band became the first jazz act named Group of the Year at the BRIT Awards. Dance, No One's Watching followed in 2024, and Here Because of Hope, released in September 2026, debuted at number one on the UK Albums Chart.

name: Everybody Loves the Sunshine
description: Everybody Loves the Sunshine is a studio album credited to Roy Ayers Ubiquity, released by Polydor Records on May 12, 1976. Produced by Roy Ayers with Maurice Green and recorded at Electric Lady Studios in New York and Larrabee Sound in West Hollywood, the album peaked at No. 51 on the Billboard 200. Its title track — built on Ayers's vibraphone and piano and a sustained synthesizer drone — became his signature song; Ayers later described its creation as spontaneous. The song has been sampled more than 100 times, in records by Mary J. Blige, Dr. Dre, and Mos Def among many others, and covered by artists including D'Angelo and the Robert Glasper Experiment. In 2016 Pitchfork placed the title track at No. 72 on its list of the 200 best songs of the 1970s. The album remains the defining statement of Ayers's jazz-funk years.

name: Ella Baker
description: Ella Josephine Baker, born in Norfolk, Virginia, in 1903 and raised in Littleton, North Carolina, graduated as valedictorian of Shaw University in 1927 and spent five decades building the infrastructure other leaders stood on. In Depression-era New York she organized consumer cooperatives; in the 1940s, as an NAACP field secretary and then director of branches, she traveled the Jim Crow South recruiting members and strengthening local chapters, growing impatient with top-down control. In 1957 she moved to Atlanta to run the new Southern Christian Leadership Conference's office and its Crusade for Citizenship voter campaign, working alongside Martin Luther King Jr. while never accepting permanent executive authority in an organization she found too centered on charismatic preaching. Her defining act came in April 1960: she convened sit-in students at Shaw University, urged them to form their own independent organization rather than a youth arm of the SCLC, and became mentor and strategist to the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee — the 'godmother of SNCC' to generations including Diane Nash, Bob Moses, and Stokely Carmichael. She later helped build the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party's 1964 challenge. Baker's teaching — that strong people do not need strong leaders — remains a working theory of grassroots democracy. She died in New York on her eighty-third birthday, December 13, 1986. Her flowers honor the organizer's organizer, who chose power shared over credit taken.

name: Earn Your Leisure
description: Earn Your Leisure is a financial-literacy podcast launched in January 2019 by Rashad Bilal, a financial adviser, and Troy Millings, a Bronx educator — friends since junior high school who first built a money curriculum for public-school students, Bilal lecturing in Millings's summer-school classes. Framed by Black Enterprise as pop culture mixed with Harvard Business School, the show breaks down investing, entrepreneurship, and the business of sports and entertainment for an underserved audience. It grew into a multifaceted platform: an online university, a podcast network, a television show, a world tour, and Invest Fest, an annual conference launched in 2021 that has drawn hundreds of thousands of attendees. Black Enterprise reports more than 50 million downloads, a peak at number one on Apple's business podcast chart, and over two million social media followers. CultureTechLens's Short covers the show; Bilal and Millings remain further gaps in the graph, named in this packet.

name: Eve
aliases: Eve Jihan Jeffers; Eve Jeffers; Eve Jihan Cooper
description: Eve (born Eve Jihan Jeffers on November 10, 1978, in Philadelphia; now Eve Jihan Cooper) is the rapper who became the Ruff Ryders' First Lady and then a three-season sitcom lead. After an early Aftermath deal collapsed, she rebuilt inside the Ruff Ryders camp and released Let There Be Eve...Ruff Ryders' First Lady (1999), which entered the Billboard 200 at number one — making her the third female rapper to top the chart — and was certified double platinum. The same year she featured on The Roots' Grammy-winning "You Got Me" and Missy Elliott's "Hot Boyz." Scorpion (2001) carried "Let Me Blow Ya Mind" with Gwen Stefani, winner of the inaugural Grammy for Best Rap/Sung Collaboration, and Eve-Olution (2002) carried "Gangsta Lovin'" with Alicia Keys. On television she played Terri Jones across the Barbershop films and starred as Shelley Williams on UPN's Eve (2003–2006). Her memoir Who's That Girl? appeared in 2024. CultureTechLens profiled Eve in Short #164.

name: Ernie Isley
description: Ernie Isley (born Ernest Isley, March 7, 1952) is an American guitarist and songwriter, the younger brother whose playing redefined the Isley Brothers' sound. Raised in Cincinnati in a musical household — a young Jimi Hendrix, then a sideman for his brothers, stayed in the family home during Ernie's childhood — he first recorded with the group at 16, playing bass on 'It's Your Thing,' and became a full member in 1973, the year his guitar drove 'That Lady.' Across the group's classic 1970s albums he wrote or co-wrote signature songs including 'Footsteps in the Dark' (1977), on which he played guitar and drums, and '(At Your Best) You Are Love' (1976). After the six-member lineup split in 1984 he returned alongside Ronald Isley in 1991 and performs with the group still. In 2024 the Guitar Center Music Foundation gave him its Lifetime Achievement Award, at which his daughter, singer Alex Isley (CTL-E-5563), performed his '(At Your Best) You Are Love.' Alex Isley's record has carried her child_of edge as blocked since Shorts Wave 2; this record is the father.

name: Eddy Curry
description: Eddy Curry, born Eddy Anthony Curry Jr. on December 5, 1982, in Harvey, Illinois, is an American former professional basketball player. At Thornwood High School in South Holland he was named Illinois Mr. Basketball and most valuable player of the McDonald's All-American Game in 2001, and the Chicago Bulls selected him fourth overall in the 2001 NBA draft directly out of high school. Curry played for Chicago from 2001 to 2005 and led the NBA in field-goal percentage in 2002–03 at .585. He then played for the New York Knicks from 2005 to 2011, won an NBA championship with the Miami Heat in 2012, and appeared briefly for Dallas before finishing his career in China with Zhejiang and, in 2018–19, Zhuhai. Across 527 NBA games he scored 6,820 points, an average of 12.9 per game.

name: Ecco2k
description: Ecco2k, born Zak Arogundade on 23 October 1994 in Stockholm, Sweden, is a Swedish singer, rapper, producer, and designer of Nigerian and Swedish heritage, and a co-founder of the Stockholm collective Drain Gang. His father is a British graphic designer, writer, and architect of Nigerian heritage; his mother is a Swedish makeup artist. He started a fashion label, Alaska, at sixteen and later worked with the sneaker brand Eytys before music took over: in 2013 he co-founded the collective — first as Gravity Boys Shield Gang — with Bladee, Whitearmor, and Yung Sherman. His solo debut album E (2019) carried his name beyond the collective, followed by the EP PXE (2021) and Crest (2022), a collaborative album with Bladee. His songs take up his position directly: the experience of being a Black man in Sweden, an insider raised there and an outsider read at a glance.

name: Everything Is Everything
description: Everything Is Everything is the debut studio album by American soul singer, songwriter, and pianist Donny Hathaway, released on July 1, 1970, on Atco Records, the Atlantic Records subsidiary. Hathaway arrived at the sessions with a Chicago grounding: after leaving Howard University in 1967 he moved to Chicago, his birthplace, and worked for Curtis Mayfield's Curtom Records as a songwriter, producer, arranger, composer, conductor, and session player before signing with Atlantic in 1969. Hathaway produced the album with drummer Ric Powell, and he wrote or co-wrote five of its nine songs. Its best-known track, "The Ghetto," was co-written with Leroy Hutson, as was the socially conscious "Tryin' Times." The remaining selections mix covers — Ray Charles's "I Believe to My Soul" and Nina Simone's "To Be Young, Gifted and Black" — with the spiritual "Thank You Master (For My Soul)" and the love song "Je Vous Aime (I Love You)." On release the album peaked at No. 73 on the Billboard Top 200 Albums chart and No. 33 on the Billboard R&B Albums chart, and Rhino's label history treats it as the solo debut of an artist who had begun as a child gospel singer under the name Donny Pitts.

name: Ethan Michaeli
description: Ethan Michaeli is an American author, journalist, and university lecturer whose first book, The Defender: How the Legendary Black Newspaper Changed America, published by Houghton Mifflin Harcourt in 2016, is a history of the Chicago Defender. His author biography records that he was born in Rochester, New York, earned a BA in English Language and Literature from the University of Chicago, and worked as a copy editor and investigative reporter at the Chicago Daily Defender from 1991 to 1996. He left the Defender to found the Residents' Journal, a magazine written and produced by tenants of Chicago's public housing developments, together with its affiliated nonprofit, We The People Media. The Defender was named a Notable Book by the New York Times, the Washington Post, and Amazon in 2016, won Best Nonfiction prizes from the Chicago Writers Association and the Midland Authors Association, and was shortlisted for the Mark Lynton Prize. His second book, Twelve Tribes: Promise and Peril in the New Israel, followed in November 2021. His biography lists him as a lecturer at the Harris School of Public Policy of the University of Chicago and a senior adviser for communications and development at the Goldin Institute, with work published by the Washington Post, the Atlantic, The Nation, and the Chicago Tribune.

name: Edwin Rosskam
description: Edwin Rosskam (1903–1985) was an American photographer, editor, and visual designer born in Munich to American parents, who came to Philadelphia in 1919 and studied painting at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts before turning to photojournalism. The African American Registry's biographical record states that he joined the Farm Security Administration and worked under Roy Stryker, designing photo exhibitions and editing documentary picture books. His defining work for Black cultural history came in 1941, when he served as photo editor — credited with photo-direction — for 12 Million Black Voices, Richard Wright's folk history of Black America published by Viking Press, selecting FSA photographs to pair with Wright's text; the Morgan Library's catalogue record confirms the 1941 Viking first edition and that its photographs were selected from the files of the Farm Security Administration. Rosskam also photographed Black Chicago directly in 1941, work later gathered in Bronzeville: Black Chicago in Pictures, 1941–1943. With his wife and collaborator Louise Rosskam he later worked on the Standard Oil photography project and a documentary initiative for the government of Puerto Rico. He died on February 25, 1985, at his home in Roosevelt, New Jersey, aged 81.

name: East-West All-Star Game
aliases: East-West Classic; Negro Leagues East-West All-Star Game
description: The East-West All-Star Game was the Negro leagues' annual showcase, first played September 10, 1933, at Comiskey Park in Chicago, where the West defeated the East 11–7 before 19,568 fans. Players were chosen by fan balloting conducted through Black newspapers; in the first vote Oscar Charleston led all players with 43,793 ballots and Willie Foster drew 40,637. Bill Foster pitched a complete game for the win and Mule Suttles hit the game's first home run. The classic ran from 1933 to 1950 and became Black America's premier recurring sporting event: the 1939 edition drew a record 40,000 fans, and the 1947 game outdrew that year's Major League Baseball All-Star Game at Wrigley Field by 7,000. Historian Larry Lester has called it the biggest event in Black America, with the sole exception of a Joe Louis fight.

name: E. Franklin Frazier
description: E. Franklin Frazier (Edward Franklin Frazier, born September 24, 1894, Baltimore; died May 17, 1962, Washington, D.C.) was the sociologist who defined the scholarly study of the Black family in America. He earned his bachelor's at Howard University in 1916, a master's at Clark in 1920, and his doctorate at the University of Chicago in 1931; the dissertation became The Negro Family in Chicago (1932), and its expansion, The Negro Family in the United States (1939), won the Anisfield-Wolf Award in 1940. He directed the Atlanta School of Social Work from 1922 to 1927, chaired Howard's sociology department, became the first Black president of the American Sociological Association in 1948, and helped draft UNESCO's 1950 statement The Race Question. His Black Bourgeoisie (French edition 1955; English 1957) remains a landmark critique, and his debate with Melville J. Herskovits over African cultural retentions structured a generation of scholarship. Howard's E. Franklin Frazier Research Center was inaugurated on May 24, 2000.

name: Elly De La Cruz
description: Elly De La Cruz, born Elly Antonio De La Cruz on 11 January 2002 in Sabana Grande de Boyá, Dominican Republic, is a Dominican switch-hitting shortstop for the Cincinnati Reds whose combination of power and speed has few precedents at his position. Signed by Cincinnati as an international free agent in 2018, he debuted on 6 June 2023 and quickly became the center of the Reds' lineup. At 6 feet 5 inches he is unusually tall for a shortstop, yet he led Major League Baseball in stolen bases in 2024 and was selected to the All-Star Game in both 2024 and 2025. In 2026 he produced the best season of his young career, batting .283 with 30 home runs and 30 stolen bases in 143 games to join Eric Davis, Barry Larkin and Brandon Phillips as the only Reds players with a 30-30 season. Through the 2026 season he had 90 career home runs and 169 stolen bases, and at 24 he remained under Cincinnati's control, with arbitration eligibility arriving in 2027.

name: Evander Holyfield
description: Evander Holyfield (born 19 October 1962 in Atmore, Alabama) is an American former professional boxer, raised in Atlanta, Georgia, who remains the only fighter to win the world heavyweight championship four separate times. After winning a bronze medal at the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, he became the first undisputed cruiserweight champion in 1988, then moved up and knocked out James 'Buster' Douglas in October 1990 to take the undisputed heavyweight title. He defended against George Foreman and Larry Holmes before trading the championship with Riddick Bowe across a celebrated trilogy, and in November 1996 he stopped Mike Tyson in the eleventh round to win the title a third time; in their June 1997 rematch Tyson was disqualified for biting his ear. Holyfield won the championship a fourth time against John Ruiz in 2000, fought on until a final bout in May 2011 in Denmark, and announced his retirement in 2014 with a record of 44 wins, 29 by knockout, 10 losses and 2 draws. He was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 2017 and has remained a public elder of the sport, giving interviews about his career and family into 2025.

name: Emmett J. Scott
description: Emmett Jay Scott, born February 13, 1873, in Houston, Texas, to formerly enslaved parents, rose from work at the Houston Post and co-founding Houston's first African American newspaper, the Texas Freeman, in 1893, to become Booker T. Washington's closest aide at Tuskegee. Hired in 1897, he served for eighteen years as Washington's confidant, personal secretary, speechwriter, and ghostwriter, became Tuskegee's treasurer-secretary in 1912, and helped Washington found the National Negro Business League in 1900. In 1917 President Woodrow Wilson appointed him special advisor on Black affairs to Secretary of War Newton Baker, described as the highest-ranking African American in a presidential administration to that point. His wartime reports were published as Scott's Official History of the American Negro in the World War in 1919 and Negro Migration during the First World War in 1920. From 1919 he served Howard University as business manager and secretary-treasurer, leaving in 1938, and during the Second World War he worked for Sun Shipbuilding in Chester, Pennsylvania. He died in Washington, D.C., in 1957, aged eighty-four.

name: Eddie Robinson
aliases: Eddie Gay Robinson Sr.; Coach Rob
description: Eddie Gay Robinson Sr. (February 13, 1919 – April 3, 2007) was the head football coach at Grambling State University in Louisiana, a historically Black university, from 1941 to 1942 and again from 1945 until his retirement in 1997. Born in Jackson, Louisiana, the son of a sharecropper and a domestic worker, Robinson earned a bachelor's degree at Leland College and a master's degree from the University of Iowa in 1954. In his second Grambling season his team went 9–0, unbeaten, untied and unscored upon. Working in an era when Southern college programs excluded Black players, he built Grambling into a national power, retiring with a record of 408 wins, 165 losses and 15 ties, 17 Southwestern Athletic Conference championships and nine Black college national championships. More than 200 of his players reached the National Football League, including Hall of Famers Buck Buchanan, Willie Brown and Charlie Joiner, and Super Bowl XXII most valuable player Doug Williams, who succeeded him in 1998. Robinson was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1997, and the Football Writers Association of America coach-of-the-year award bears his name.

name: Ethel Waters
description: Ethel Waters (1896-1977) was an American blues singer and actress. After singing in a local nightclub, she joined the Braxton and Nugent vaudeville troupe performing regionally around Baltimore and became an overnight sensation singing 'St. Louis Blues,' the only woman to have done so at that time, before establishing herself as a recording artist and touring nationally. In 1933 she accepted an offer to perform at New York's Cotton Club, where she introduced 'Stormy Weather' in the Cotton Club Parade, singing it with Duke Ellington and his orchestra; the performance was a turning point that led Irving Berlin to offer her a role in his Broadway revue As Thousands Cheer. She became the first African American woman to integrate Broadway and soon one of the highest paid actresses on Broadway regardless of race. Her Broadway acclaim led to film, including Cabin in the Sky (1943), and to television. She was the second African American to be nominated for an Academy Award — for Pinky (1949) — the first African American to star in her own television show, and the first African American woman to be nominated for a Primetime Emmy Award. She died on September 1, 1977.

name: Elinor Tatum
description: Elinor Ruth Tatum (born January 29, 1971, in New York City) is the publisher and editor-in-chief of the New York Amsterdam News, one of the oldest and most influential Black newspapers in the United States. The daughter of former Amsterdam News publisher Wilbert Tatum, she graduated from St. Lawrence University in 1993 with a degree in government studies, studied international relations at Stockholm University, and returned to New York to join her father's paper as assistant to the publisher. The HistoryMakers records her promotion to associate publisher and chief operating officer in 1996, her master's degree in journalism from New York University in 1997, and her promotion that year to publisher and editor-in-chief, making her one of the youngest publishers in the history of the African American press. After her father's death in 2009 she assumed full control of the newspaper. Under her leadership the paper modernized, adding an online edition and a new layout. She has also produced and co-hosted a weekly segment on Al Sharpton's radio program and served on civic and university boards. A 2026 Harlem Community News account of the Amsterdam News describes its current masthead as still led by publisher Elinor Tatum, confirming her in the role in 2026.

name: Edmonia Lewis
description: Mary Edmonia Lewis was a nineteenth-century sculptor of African American and Native American descent, born in Greenbush, New York, in 1844, to a Black father and a Chippewa (Ojibwa) mother. Orphaned young, she was raised among her mother's people, where she was known as Wildfire, and in 1859 she entered Oberlin College, among the first American schools to admit women and Black students. An accusation of poisoning, described by the Smithsonian as probably racially motivated, forced her to leave before graduating. In Boston she trained with a local sculptor and built a practice making portraits of antislavery heroes; sales of her bust of Colonel Robert Gould Shaw, over one hundred plaster copies in one museum account, helped finance her move to Rome in 1865. There she joined a circle of American women sculptors and worked in marble, doing her own stonework so her authorship could not be doubted. Her subjects ranged across biblical scenes, her Native heritage and the oppression of Black people, including Forever Free, Hagar and The Death of Cleopatra. She died in London in 1907.

name: Edward W. Brooke
aliases: Edward William Brooke III; Edward Brooke; Senator Brooke
description: Edward William Brooke III (1919–2015) was a Republican senator from Massachusetts and the first African American elected to the United States Senate by popular vote. Born in Washington, D.C., in 1919, he graduated from Howard University in 1941 and served in the segregated, all-Black 366th Infantry Regiment during World War II, earning the rank of captain and a Bronze Star. After earning law degrees from Boston University, he built a practice in Boston's Roxbury neighborhood, chaired the Boston Finance Commission, and in 1962 became the first African American elected a state's attorney general. Elected to the Senate in 1966 with about 60 percent of the vote, he served two terms, from 1967 to 1979, as the Senate's only Black member during the civil rights era. He co-sponsored, with Walter Mondale, the fair housing provision that became the key title of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, defended school desegregation, and in November 1973 became the first Republican senator to call publicly for President Nixon's resignation. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2004 and the Congressional Gold Medal, presented in 2009. He died in January 2015.

name: Emerald South Economic Development Collaborative
description: The Emerald South Economic Development Collaborative is a Chicago place-based economic development organization working to generate community wealth on the city's mid-South Side. This is a Chicago record: its mission is to attract and coordinate investment through community convening and collaborative partnerships that increase local ownership and prosperity across neighborhoods including Woodlawn, South Shore, and Washington Park. President and CEO Ghian Foreman has said the collaborative was created by community leaders together with the University of Chicago, the City of Chicago, and the Obama Foundation so that surrounding neighborhoods would share in the economic benefit of the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park. The organization's own figures report more than 70,000 residents served through community initiatives, more than 100 acres of vacant land maintained and fenced, and more than 75 businesses, nonprofits, and other organizations enrolled in a group-purchasing program. Its Terra Firma initiative, launched in 2021 as a $50 million land-care effort, has stabilized 102 acres across some 600 parcels in nine neighborhoods, supported 41 community gardens, and directed $2.3 million to local minority contractors.

name: Erskine Tate
description: Erskine Tate was an American jazz violinist and bandleader born January 14, 1895, in Memphis, Tennessee. He moved to Chicago in 1912 and became an early figure on the Chicago jazz scene. At the Vendome Theater, a movie house at 31st and State Street, his Vendome Theater Symphony Orchestra accompanied silent films and played classical and light repertoire alongside jazz; the University of Chicago Library's exhibition history records his thirteen-piece Vendome Theater Orchestra as the theater's resident band from 1919 to 1928, with Louis Armstrong a member in 1926. Musicians who passed through Tate's orchestra included Freddie Keppard, Buster Bailey, Jimmy Bertrand, Ed Atkins, Teddy Weatherford, Fats Waller, and Teddy Wilson. Documented overtures at the Vendome included works associated with Franz von Suppé and Gioacchino Rossini, alongside music by Wagner and Beethoven. In the mid-1930s Tate retired from active performance and became a music teacher, remaining a Chicago music educator in later decades. He died December 17, 1978, in Chicago, aged 83.

name: Eve's Bayou
description: Eve's Bayou is a 1997 American film written and directed by Kasi Lemmons, her feature directorial debut. It was among the first films to showcase the beauty of African American Southern culture, in the account given by the Sundance Institute. Samuel L. Jackson, who starred in the film, also made his debut as a film producer on the picture, and the film helped launch the careers of actresses Meagan Good and Jurnee Smollett. It received the Independent Spirit Award for Best First Feature, and the National Board of Review gave Lemmons a special award for a first-time director. In 2018 the film was added to the National Film Registry of the Library of Congress, ensuring its preservation as a work of cultural, historic, and aesthetic importance to the nation's film heritage. Lemmons, who teaches in the Graduate Film Department at New York University's Tisch School of the Arts, said in a statement carried by the university that, as a Black woman filmmaker, the Library of Congress recognition of the film's diversity of culture, perspective, and expression was particularly meaningful to her and to future generations of filmmakers.

name: Evelyn Cunningham
aliases: Evelyn Elizabeth Long; The Lynching Editor
description: Evelyn Cunningham (January 25, 1916 – April 28, 2010) was an American journalist born Evelyn Elizabeth Long in Elizabeth City, North Carolina, and raised in New York City, where she graduated from Long Island University in 1943. She joined the Pittsburgh Courier in 1940 and worked mostly from its New York office until 1962, as its New York City editor and a columnist, including the column “The Women.” Her extensive coverage of lynchings in the segregated South earned her the nickname “the lynching editor.” She reported on the Montgomery bus boycott, school desegregation in Birmingham, and the killings of Black sharecroppers who had voted, interviewed Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X, and wrote a three-part series on the King family. In 1998 she was among the former Courier reporters who accepted the George Polk Career Award on behalf of the paper for its civil rights coverage, the first time the award went to a publication rather than an individual. She later hosted a WLIB radio program, served as special assistant to Governor Nelson Rockefeller and director of the state's Women's Unit, advised him during his vice presidency, and in 1970 co-founded the Coalition of 100 Black Women. She died in Manhattan at ninety-four.
